PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-kV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT
WRITTEN POLICY BRIEF OF NELDA HOWTON REGARDING PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS, NOTICE, AND MEANINGFUL LANDOWNER PARTICIPATION
Submitted for Commission consideration of procedural safeguards; not to reopen the evidentiary record or argue the merits of a particular route.
I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
Nelda Howton submits this written policy brief as an affected Texas landowner and pro se participant who has personally experienced the transmission-line certificate process in PUC Docket No. 59475. The purpose of this paper is not to ask the Commission to reconsider the merits of a particular route. It is to identify procedural lessons from that experience and recommend safeguards that would give every affected landowner a fair, transparent, and meaningful opportunity to participate before decisions become irreversible.
The Commission's procedural rules already recognize that public participation, notice, and an opportunity to be heard are essential parts of a contested case. PURA §12.202 directs the Commission to provide the public a reasonable opportunity to appear and speak on matters within its jurisdiction, and Texas Government Code §2001.051 protects a party's opportunity to respond and present evidence and argument. The issue raised here is whether the practical operation of the transmission-line process gives later-affected, rural, elderly, and unrepresented landowners a genuinely comparable opportunity to use those rights.
II. SUMMARY OF THE PROCEDURAL CONCERNS
Mrs. Howton's experience identified several connected problems: notice may technically comply with a filing-based deadline while leaving a newly affected landowner only a short period to learn the process; a materially changed or later-added route can bring new landowners into the case after the public-participation process has already occurred; utilities may rely heavily on desktop, aerial, GIS, database, and mapping information before local facts have been verified on the ground; and ordinary landowners may discover errors or important questions only after the procedural schedule has advanced beyond the point at which those matters can be meaningfully developed.
Mrs. Howton's prior filings explained that landowners on earlier routes had many months to study the Environmental Assessment, review maps, identify omissions, coordinate with neighbors, retain counsel or experts, and advocate regarding routing decisions. Later-affected landowners entered after the process had already been substantially shaped and had a compressed period in which to do the same work. Her written testimony also emphasized that aerial photographs and databases cannot reliably show every fact that matters on working rural property: occupancy, actual land use, livestock and equipment movement, access, community use of a church or gathering place, storm-recovery conditions, and other local circumstances may require direct verification.
III. MEANINGFUL NOTICE SHOULD BE MEASURED BY PRACTICAL OPPORTUNITY, NOT ONLY BY A FILING DATE
For a new transmission facility subject to PURA §37.057, current 16 TAC §22.104(b)(1) generally requires a motion to intervene within 30 days from the date the application is filed. Section 22.52 likewise requires notice to directly affected landowners when the application is filed. That structure is administratively clear, but it does not necessarily measure how much time a landowner actually has after receiving and understanding the notice.
The rules themselves already recognize the importance of actual receipt in one circumstance. Under 16 TAC §22.104(d)(4), when a directly affected landowner did not receive required direct notice, late intervention is available as a matter of right if the person acts within 15 days of actually receiving notice, and the rule states that the person should be afforded sufficient time to prepare for and participate in the proceeding. That principle should inform the ordinary notice process as well. A person who receives technically timely mailed notice but has only a few weeks to learn a highly specialized administrative process still faces a substantial practical disadvantage.
Mrs. Howton therefore asks the Commission to consider a receipt-based minimum preparation period for directly affected landowners. She has previously proposed 90 days from actual receipt of notice to the intervention deadline when the governing statutory schedule permits. At a minimum, the Commission should consider an automatic procedure that preserves a meaningful preparation period when a landowner is first brought into the case late in the route-development process.
IV. A MATERIAL ROUTE CHANGE SHOULD CREATE A NEW PARTICIPATION OPPORTUNITY
Current 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) requires at least one pre-filing public meeting when 25 or more persons would be entitled to direct mailed notice. Section 22.52(a)(3)(D) also requires notice to newly directly affected landowners before final approval of a route modification. These protections are important, but they do not expressly guarantee that a newly affected group will receive a comparable public-meeting opportunity when a material route or link is added after the original public meeting.
That is a meaningful procedural gap. A landowner cannot participate in a public meeting about a route that did not yet affect that landowner. If a material route change creates a new group of directly affected owners, the process should provide more than notice that the change has already occurred. The new group should receive a comparable opportunity to ask questions, identify local facts, communicate concerns, and provide information before the matter is locked into a compressed contested-case schedule.
Mrs. Howton asks the Commission to require supplemental notice and a renewed participation period whenever an applicant adds, relocates, or materially changes a route or link in a way that directly affects previously uninvolved landowners. If the change occurs after the public meeting, the Commission should consider requiring a supplemental meeting or an equivalent formal participation process for the newly affected group.
V. LANDOWNERS SHOULD HAVE A FORMAL DATA-VERIFICATION PERIOD BEFORE THE EVIDENTIARY HEARING
A central lesson from Mrs. Howton's experience is that accurate routing information cannot always be developed from a computer screen. Utilities understandably use aerial photography, GIS layers, county records, agency databases, and other desktop tools. Those resources are necessary, but they are not a substitute for local verification when the information will be used to make a permanent routing decision.
An aerial image may not establish whether a structure is occupied, how a family actually uses its property, how cattle, horses, farm equipment, or emergency vehicles move across the land, whether a local church serves as a significant community gathering place, or whether recent storm damage has changed conditions on the ground. Mrs. Howton's prior testimony specifically emphasized these limitations and asked that reliable information be gathered before a route is proposed rather than after landowners are required to defend their homes in a legal proceeding.
The Commission should consider requiring the applicant to provide each directly affected landowner with a simple property-information sheet identifying the facts the applicant intends to use about that property: habitable structures, land use, known community or cultural resources, environmental features, and other material routing information. The landowner should then receive a defined period to identify factual errors or omissions before the evidentiary hearing. Material disputes could be flagged for field verification rather than first discovered during cross-examination.
VI. FIELD VERIFICATION SHOULD BE DOCUMENTED BEFORE ROUTING DATA IS RELIED UPON
Mrs. Howton has previously requested documented boots-on-the-ground inspections before proposed routes are filed with the Commission. The requested safeguard is not that every inch of every alternative must be physically walked. Rather, where route selection depends on facts that can materially affect the comparison—such as habitable structures, actual land use, access, community resources, or environmental and cultural features—the record should show what was field-verified, by whom, when, and what remained based only on desktop information.
A documented verification protocol would help the Commission distinguish between verified facts and preliminary assumptions. It would also reduce later disputes, improve the reliability of the Environmental Assessment, and allow the people who know the land best to correct mistakes before the hearing schedule becomes the limiting factor.
VII. ROUTE-CHANGE TRANSPARENCY AND EQUAL ACCESS SHOULD BE STRENGTHENED
Current 16 TAC §22.52(a)(3)(E) requires proof of landowner notice to include a statement of whether any formal contact related to the proceeding occurred between the utility and the landowner beyond the required notice. That requirement recognizes that contacts outside the standard notice process can matter. Mrs. Howton respectfully asks the Commission to make the disclosure more useful.
When a material route or link changes after communications with a landowner, attorney, developer, governmental entity, or other interested person, the public record should identify the date of the communication, the participants, the subject of the request, the change requested, and whether the communication affected the routing decision. The purpose is not to presume wrongdoing. It is to ensure equal access and public confidence. Similarly situated landowners should be able to see what information influenced a material change and have a fair opportunity to provide responsive information.
The Commission should also consider requiring a short Route Change Report for every material change. The report could identify the prior alignment, the revised alignment, the date of the change, the decision participants, the objective routing factors considered, material outside communications, and a concise explanation of why the change was made.
VIII. THE PROCESS SHOULD BE ACCESSIBLE TO RURAL, ELDERLY, AND PRO SE LANDOWNERS
The Commission's rules recognize that not every participant has internet or email access, including through the Statement of No Access procedure and non-email service options. That is important, but the practical burdens extend beyond receiving documents. A first-time landowner must understand intervention, discovery, testimony, exhibits, service, filing requirements, hearing procedures, and deadlines—often while continuing to manage a farm, job, family, health problem, or storm recovery.
Mrs. Howton's filings noted that some elderly rural neighbors did not own computers or did not know how to research the proceeding and complete the necessary forms. The process should not unintentionally reward those who already have lawyers, technical consultants, regulatory experience, or early access to routing information.
Mrs. Howton asks the Commission to expand plain-language instructions, telephone assistance, paper options, and simple checklists explaining what a landowner must do at each stage. Newly affected landowners should receive a concise explanation of the procedural schedule, the consequences of intervention versus filing comments, how to obtain the Environmental Assessment and maps, how to correct property information, and how to preserve an issue for the record.
IX. EXISTING CORRIDORS AND IMPACTS TO PRIVATE PROPERTY SHOULD BE EXPLAINED IN WRITING
Mrs. Howton has also previously asked for greater transparency when a new routing burden is placed near homes, farms, churches, schools, or established communities even though existing transmission corridors or other compatible rights-of-way may be available. This policy concern is not a request for the Commission to choose a specific route in this paper. It is a request for a documented explanation.
When an applicant selects or retains an alignment that imposes a new burden on private property instead of using or paralleling an existing compatible corridor, the application should briefly state what existing-corridor options were evaluated and the objective reason they were not used. Likewise, when a route near an existing residence is selected over an available alternative that appears to create less residential impact, the record should contain a clear written explanation of the routing criteria that drove that choice. A transparent explanation allows the Commission and affected owners to evaluate the decision without speculation.
X. REQUESTED COMMISSION SAFEGUARDS
Based on these experiences, Mrs. Howton respectfully requests that the Commission consider the following prospective procedural safeguards for transmission-line CCN proceedings:
1. Receipt-based meaningful notice. Establish a minimum preparation period measured from actual receipt of notice for newly affected landowners. Mrs. Howton has proposed 90 days when the statutory schedule permits, or otherwise the longest practical receipt-based period consistent with the governing deadline.
2. Renewed participation after material route changes. Require supplemental notice and a renewed participation period when a route or link is added, relocated, or materially changed in a way that directly affects previously uninvolved landowners.
3. Supplemental public participation. When a material change occurs after the original public meeting, require a supplemental public meeting or an equivalent formal opportunity for newly affected landowners to participate before the hearing schedule substantially advances.
4. Landowner verification period. Provide directly affected landowners a property-information summary and a defined opportunity to correct material errors in structure counts, land use, community-resource information, and environmental descriptions before the evidentiary hearing.
5. Documented field verification. Require applicants to identify which material routing facts were verified on the ground, the date and method of verification, and which facts remain based on desktop or third-party data.
6. Route Change Report. Require a written audit trail for material route changes identifying when the change occurred, who participated, what objective criteria were considered, what material outside communications were received, and why the change was made.
7. More complete contact disclosure. Expand the current proof-of-notice disclosure regarding formal contacts so that material route-related communications are described with enough detail to permit equal and transparent participation.
8. Rural, elderly, and pro se access. Provide plain-language instructions, telephone and paper options, no-internet accommodations, and a procedural checklist specifically designed for first-time landowner intervenors.
9. Written corridor and private-property explanation. Require a concise written explanation when an applicant does not use or parallel an available compatible corridor, or when a routing decision places a new burden near an existing home or community resource despite an apparently less-impactful alternative.
XI. CONCLUSION
Texas needs a reliable electric grid, and Mrs. Howton does not contend otherwise. But the need to build infrastructure should not require ordinary landowners to enter a highly technical legal process after the important decisions have already been shaped and then discover, too late, what questions they should have asked or what information they should have corrected.
A home is more than a point on a utility map. For a rural family, it can represent decades of work, livestock and agricultural activity, family history, security, and property intended for children and grandchildren. When government authorizes infrastructure that can permanently affect that property, the process should be designed to produce confidence as well as a decision.
Mrs. Howton respectfully asks the Commission to strengthen the transmission-line process around five basic principles: meaningful notice, equal participation, accurate information, transparent decision-making, and practical access for ordinary Texans. These safeguards would not guarantee any landowner a particular routing outcome. They would help ensure that every affected landowner has a fair opportunity to be heard before a permanent decision is made.
Respectfully submitted,
NELDA HOWTON
Pro Se Intervenor, Party No. 250
Salado, Bell County, Texas
Contact information as on file in PUC Docket No. 59475
